question: A good cushion of space separating you from other vehicles gives you what two main benefits?
choice_a: A legal exemption from following-distance rules
choice_b: A quieter ride and better fuel economy
choice_c: More time to respond and more space to maneuver, including an escape path
explanation: A cushion of space provides a clear view of traffic situations, so if someone else makes a mistake you have more time to respond and more space to maneuver, including an escape path if necessary.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.11, 'Keeping Your Distance'

question: Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle how many paths of travel to choose from?
explanation: Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel -- the left, center, and right portions of the lane -- and no portion of the lane needs to be avoided, including the center.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.11-12, 'Lane Positions'

question: Why does the manual say to be cautious of the center third of the lane, even though it usually has adequate traction?
choice_a: Debris, oil drippings, and surface hazards tend to collect there
choice_b: It is the only part of the lane where riding is illegal
choice_c: It has no traction whatsoever, even when dry
choice_d: It is always closer to oncoming traffic
explanation: The center third of the lane is where debris and oil drippings from cars collect and where hazards such as surface covers are located, though unless the road is wet the typical center strip permits adequate traction.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.12, 'Lane Positions'

question: What is described as one absolute for lane positioning that experienced riders rely on?
choice_a: Always ride in the far right portion of the lane
choice_b: Avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot
choice_c: Always ride in the far left portion of the lane
choice_d: Always match the speed of the vehicle ahead exactly
explanation: Experienced riders rely on their own strategies and judgment for lane position, but one absolute is to avoid riding in another vehicle's blind spot.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.12, 'Lane Positions'

question: Normally, what minimum following distance should be maintained behind a vehicle?
choice_a: Five car lengths regardless of speed
explanation: Following too closely is a frequent factor in motorcyclist crashes. Normally, a minimum of two seconds distance should be maintained when following a vehicle.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.12, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: To gauge your following distance, what should you do after the vehicle ahead passes a fixed marker?
choice_a: Speed up until you can read the vehicle's license plate
choice_b: Estimate distance in car lengths only
choice_c: Flash your high beam and count the flashes
choice_d: Count off the seconds -- if you reach the marker before counting to two, you are following too closely
explanation: Pick a marker on or near the road ahead. When the vehicle ahead passes it, count off the seconds; if you reach the marker before you reach two seconds, you are following too closely.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.13, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: When should a rider open up a three-second or more following distance?
choice_a: If the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or traffic is heavy
choice_b: Only when riding a borrowed motorcycle
choice_d: A three-second distance is never necessary
explanation: A larger cushion of space is needed if your motorcycle will take longer than normal to stop -- if the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front of you, open up a three-second or more following distance.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.13, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: When riding behind a car, where should you position yourself so the driver can see you in their mirror?
choice_a: Directly against the vehicle's rear bumper
choice_b: In the center portion of the lane, visible in the inside rearview mirror
choice_c: In the driver's blind spot, since it is closer
choice_d: It doesn't matter -- drivers always check their sideview mirrors first
explanation: When behind a car, ride where the driver can see you in the inside rearview mirror. Riding in the center portion of the lane should put you in view, since most drivers check the inside mirror far more often than sideview mirrors.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.13, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: What does the manual recommend as a better way to handle a tailgater than speeding up?
choice_b: Speed up until they can no longer keep pace
choice_c: Try to get them to pass you, or slow down and open extra space ahead to encourage them to pass
choice_d: Change lanes only after they have already passed
explanation: Speeding up to lose a tailgater can end with them tailgating at a higher speed. A better way is to get them in front of you -- let them pass, or slow down and open extra space ahead to encourage them to pass.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.13-14, 'Being Followed'

question: When passing another vehicle, after moving into the left lane and accelerating, what should a rider avoid doing?
choice_a: Returning to the original lane after completing the pass
choice_d: Lingering in the blind spot of the vehicle being passed
explanation: After moving into the left lane and accelerating, don't linger in the blind spot; signal again, complete mirror and head checks, then return to the original lane and cancel the signal.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.14, 'Passing'

question: When being passed from behind, where should you position yourself in your lane?
choice_a: Stay in the center portion of your lane
choice_b: Move as close as possible to the passing vehicle
choice_c: Move to the far edge of the lane nearest the passing vehicle
choice_d: Come to a stop until the vehicle finishes passing
explanation: When you are being passed from behind, stay in the center portion of your lane -- riding close to the passing vehicle could put you in a hazardous situation.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.14, 'Being Passed'

question: Why should you watch out for a vehicle's "extended mirrors" when being passed?
choice_a: Extended mirrors are illegal in Minnesota
choice_b: Some drivers forget their mirrors hang out farther than their fenders
choice_c: They always indicate the vehicle is about to turn
choice_d: They block the passing driver's view completely
explanation: When being passed, consider extended mirrors -- some drivers forget that their mirrors hang out farther than their fenders, which can create a hazard for a rider positioned too close.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.14-15, 'Being Passed'

question: What risk does the manual describe with riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane (lane sharing)?
choice_a: It only creates a legal risk, never a physical one
choice_b: It is always perfectly safe if done slowly
choice_c: A hand could come out of a window, a door could open, or a car could turn suddenly
choice_d: It is required by law in heavy traffic
explanation: Riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane can leave you vulnerable to the unexpected -- a hand could come out of a window, a door could open, or a car could turn suddenly. Lane sharing is usually prohibited.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.15, 'Lane Sharing'

question: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze past a motorcycle in the same lane in which of these situations?
choice_a: Never -- lane sharing attempts by other drivers are extremely rare
choice_c: Only when the motorcycle has its headlight off
choice_d: In heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic, or when they want to pass
explanation: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze by a motorcycle in heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic, when they want to pass, when the rider is preparing to turn at an intersection, or when moving into an exit lane.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.15, 'Lane Sharing'

question: When a vehicle is merging onto the highway from an entrance ramp, what should a rider do?
choice_a: Give the merging vehicle plenty of room, changing lanes if possible or adjusting speed
choice_b: Speed up to pass the ramp before the vehicle merges
choice_c: Assume the merging driver has already seen you
choice_d: Move closer to the merging vehicle to be more visible
explanation: Drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway. Give them plenty of room -- change to another lane if one is open, or adjust speed to open up space for the merging vehicle.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.15, 'Merging Vehicles'

question: Why does the manual advise against riding next to cars or trucks in other lanes when you don't have to?
choice_a: It is against the law in every state
choice_b: You might be in a blind spot, and a vehicle could switch lanes without warning while also blocking your escape route
choice_c: It uses more fuel than riding behind traffic
choice_d: It has no real downside, only benefits
explanation: Do not ride next to cars or trucks in other lanes if you don't have to -- you might be in the blind spot and a vehicle could switch into your lane without warning, and vehicles alongside also block your escape if you come upon danger in your own lane.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.15-16, 'Vehicles Alongside'

question: Why does the manual say to keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are stopped?
choice_a: It is required only when a passenger is aboard
choice_b: It is only a courtesy with no safety purpose
choice_c: It makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind, and gives a cushion if the vehicle ahead backs up
choice_d: It has no effect on a rider's ability to escape a rear hazard
explanation: Keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are stopped. This will make it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind, and gives a cushion of space if the vehicle ahead starts to back up for some reason.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.13-14, 'Following Another Vehicle'
